overview: This two-page Department of State list of papers indexes ten records concerning the government of the Kwantung Leased Territory. The entries, principally reports from U.S. officials in Dairen, Japan, Nanking, and China, concern Japanese administrative reorganization in Manchuria, the new governmental system instituted in the leased territory in December 1934, personnel changes, a proposed transfer of the territorial government from Port Arthur to Dairen, and broader reports on conditions in the territory. Several entries are notes or cross-references directing researchers to related decimal-file records rather than copies of the underlying documents.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Government of Kwantung
subfiles.about: An index of diplomatic papers and cross-references concerning the government and administrative reorganization of the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The list records items numbered 76 through 85, including reports by Perkins, Vincent, Neville, Grummon, and Atcheson. Its subjects include Cai Tinggan's favorable opinion of Japanese administration, the reorganization of Japanese agencies in Manchuria, military control of Japanese representation there, and the new Kwantung governmental system instituted in December 1934. Later entries concern personnel changes, the proposed transfer of the territorial government from Port Arthur to Dairen, and general reports on the leased territory. The list also points to related records in decimal files 893.00, 893.01-Manchuria, 894.002, and 894C.00.

interest: The document is useful less for substantive detail than as a map of U.S. diplomatic reporting on Japanese colonial administration in southern Manchuria. It identifies records that may have been filed elsewhere, including precise decimal-file references, and traces a cluster of administrative changes during 1934–1935, notably the establishment of a new governmental system and a contemplated move from Port Arthur to Dairen. It also preserves an unusual reference to Chinese admiral Cai Tinggan's admiration for Japanese administration, offering a lead for research into Chinese elite perceptions of colonial governance.
